The applicants were represented by Mr [PERSON], a lawyer practising in Lincoln. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) was represented by their Agents. The Court decided to examine the merits of the applications and their admissibility. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant, a soldier of the regular forces of the British Army, was charged with wounding with intent contrary to section 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act. The convening officer convened a general court-martial. The applicant was found guilty on the first charge and of assault occasioning actual bodily harm. He was sentenced to imprisonment and to be discharged from the army. The second applicant argued before the single judge that the judge advocate had erred and misdirected the court. The single judge granted leave to appeal to the full CMAC. His petition against sentence to the confirming officer was rejected and his conviction and sentence were promulgated. By letter dated [DATE_TIME], his representatives were informed of the decision. It was also indicated in that letter that the “PERSON’s issue” had been frequently rejected by the Reviewing Authority and by the CMAC. The Court of Appeal ruled that the decision to reject the appeal had been made in accordance with Article 6 of the Convention. The CMAC considered that there was no chain of command influence and no obvious reason why any observer would suspect any lack of independence or impartiality. The applicants' reliance on the [PERSON] judgment was misconceived as the only power of the CMAC was to enquire as to whether the convictions were unsafe. It noted that the time for having regard to the provisions of the Convention had not yet been reached, but it was difficult to see, even in such circumstances, how the provisions could be of any assistance to the applicants.
